analysis.one_liner: Bans firing or refusing to hire workers for being gay or transgender.
analysis.headline: The Employment Non-Discrimination Act drew 43 Senate cosponsors and a committee hearing in June 2012, but never received a Senate vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added sexual orientation and gender identity to federal employment anti-discrimination law, alongside race, sex, religion, and national origin. It would have made it illegal for employers with 15 or more workers, employment agencies, and unions to fire, refuse to hire, or otherwise mistreat someone because of their actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity, and it gave workers the same complaint process and remedies they already have under the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues, got one hearing, and never reached the floor for a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender workers, and anyone whose employer suspects them of being so. At the time, in most states it was legal to fire a worker for being gay or transgender, and this bill would have given those workers a federal remedy. State and federal government employees would have been covered too.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers with 15 or more employees, employment agencies, and labor organizations from firing, refusing to hire, or otherwise discriminating against a worker because of actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity, including discrimination based on who a worker associates with.

Gives workers the same enforcement machinery and remedies they have under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Justice Department, and federal courts handling claims the same way as race or sex discrimination cases.
Covers federal, state, and congressional employees, and lets state workers sue even over their states' immunity from suit, as long as no punitive damages are awarded.
Bars retaliation against workers who file complaints, testify, or assist in an investigation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees would face new liability and the cost of compliance, including posting workplace notices, though the bill explicitly bans quotas and preferential treatment, allows employers to keep uniform dress and grooming rules, and does not require building new facilities.

drawbacks.text: Religious organizations are fully exempt, so faith-affiliated employers could continue making employment decisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
The bill defines marriage using the Defense of Marriage Act, then federal law, so it would not have required employers to treat a worker's same-sex spouse as married for benefits purposes.

Workers could bring only disparate-treatment claims, not claims that a facially neutral practice has a discriminatory impact, and lawsuits against the federal or state governments could not seek punitive damages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: before the Supreme Court's 2020 ruling that sex discrimination in Title VII covers sexual orientation and gender identity, workers in most states could legally be fired for being gay or transgender, and this bill offered them a federal complaint process they did not otherwise have. The costs to employers are comparatively modest because the bill borrows existing civil-rights procedures and rules out quotas. The genuine weaknesses are the carve-outs: religious employers are exempt and the bill would have written DOMA's definition of marriage into employee benefits, so protection would have been incomplete even if enacted.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the labor committee, which held one hearing, and the bill never came up for a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2011 by Senator Jeff Merkley with two Republicans, Senators Mark Kirk and Susan Collins, and Democrat Tom Harkin as original cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
It accumulated 43 cosponsors in the Senate, including 3 Republicans, 38 Democrats, and 2 independents.
The committee held its only hearing on June 12, 2012, and the bill was never reported out of committee or scheduled for a Senate vote.
No version of the bill received a vote in either chamber during the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and religious organizations that prefer no federal sexual-orientation and gender-identity employment rules are better off, because the bill died without a vote and no national standard was created in the 112th Congress. Workers in states without their own protections gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that avoided the new rules

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at introduction — 38 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 2 independents cosponsored — and the bill died without any recorded floor opposition, simply never reaching a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have created a new federal cause of action against them for sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination, with Title VII-style procedures and remedies. Their interest in avoiding that liability runs against workers' interest in not being fired for who they are.

The bill would have carved them out entirely, preserving their existing exemption from religious-discrimination rules under Title VII. That exemption leaves workers at faith-affiliated employers without this protection.
They would have been covered as employers and referral sources, barred from excluding or classifying members or referrals by sexual orientation or gender identity.
